title: How to make a medical device video that physicians watch
overview: How to make a medical device video: planning medical device video production, from procedure filming and animation to training videos and sales enablement content.
author: Made Clear
body:
Learning how to make a medical device video that physicians actually watch starts with one decision: what should the viewer understand or do when it ends? Medical device video production covers everything from a 30-second social clip to a full procedural training film, and each needs a different approach. Get the purpose right and the rest follows.

Here's how we approach medtech video production, from first brief to final delivery.

1. Define the audience and the job

A video for interventional cardiologists, one for cath lab nurses and one for hospital administrators will look very different. So will a launch film, a training video and a sales tool. Write down who will watch, where and why, before thinking about style.

2. Choose the right mix of formats

Most strong device videos combine several elements:

  • Procedure footage: the device in real use, filmed in the cath lab or theatre.
  • Animation: to show what happens inside the body, which no camera can capture.
  • KOL interviews: physicians explaining why and when they use the device.
  • Product shots: clean, detailed footage of the device itself.
  • Physical models: sometimes a real demonstration beats CGI. For Big Discrepancies, Big Solutions, we filmed iVascular's Angiolite stent expanding inside transparent artery models, guided by a trained cardiologist on set.

3. Surgical procedure video production

Filming procedures needs a crew that understands clinical environments: sterile fields, patient consent and confidentiality, radiation, limited space and a team that can't be interrupted. Plan camera positions with the clinical team, capture imaging feeds alongside the room cameras and keep the crew small. For Philips ICE in the Heart, we filmed two leading interventional cardiologists performing the LAAO procedure in their own cath labs, then paired the footage with short interviews on the device's benefits.

4. Plan the story and the script

Even a technical film needs a structure. Open with the clinical problem, show how the device solves it, then prove it with footage, data or a physician's experience. Agree the script and storyboard with medical and regulatory reviewers before filming, so the shoot captures exactly what's needed and late changes are avoided.

5. Medical device training videos

Medical device training videos have to be precise and easy to follow. Break the procedure into clear steps, show each from the most useful angle and combine live footage with animation where the anatomy is hard to see. The Philips ICE project included a detailed medical-grade animation of the end-to-end procedure, designed to give physicians, radiographers and cath lab staff the procedural knowledge they need without additional training.

  • One step per scene, with clear on-screen labels.
  • Short chapters people can return to, rather than one long film.
  • Subtitles, so the video works in a noisy hospital or on a phone.

Chaptering works for patients too: our HCA UK patient education film was built as 13 short standalone chapters.

6. Sales rep training and sales enablement

Sales rep training for medical devices and medical device sales enablement content serve two purposes: helping reps understand the device, and giving them something compelling to show physicians. The best sales tools are short, visual and easy to run on a tablet in a hospital corridor. Some go further: The Curious Case of Coronary Calcium, a VR experience presented by two leading interventional cardiologists, is used as a field sales tool by Shockwave's commercial teams. At South West Calcium, we trained Shockwave's local team to run the headsets themselves, so the experience could travel to future meetings.

7. Capture more than one video

A production day is expensive to set up, so plan to get several pieces from it: a hero film, short cuts for social, training chapters, KOL clips and stills. Congresses are especially efficient. At TCT 2026, an always-on filming booth on Shockwave Medical's stand captured KOLs, physicians and leadership throughout the congress.

8. Review, version and distribute

  • Allow time for medical, legal and regulatory review.
  • Plan language versions and different lengths up front.
  • Decide where each version will live: congress screens, education platforms, the field team's tablets, LinkedIn.
  • Measure what matters: watch time, completion and what the field team hears back.

Getting started

Start with the purpose and the audience, then build the production around them. If you're planning a medical device video, see our medical film and documentary work or get in touch.
